changed_graph.name: CO2 Fixation and Sucrose Production
changed_graph.description: CscB+ S. elongatus fixes carbon and exports sucrose, but E. coli W and W delta-cscR grew during early batch coculture independently of induced sucrose export. The source infers substantial use of other photosynthates at that stage; their identities, including the proposed extracellular polymers, were not resolved. The earlier 85% carbon-export capability is not a concentration or a measurement of this dyad.

downstream.target: E. coli growth on cyanobacterial photosynthate
downstream.description: Cyanobacterial photosynthate supports E. coli growth. PARTIAL for sucrose-specific mediation: early growth was insensitive to export induction, so that phase cannot be attributed solely to sucrose; later productive cocultures show a sucrose contribution.

evidence.snippet: We previously engineered a model cyanobacterium, Synechococcus elongatus PCC 7942, to secrete the bulk of the carbon it fixes as sucrose, a carbohydrate that can be utilized by many other microbes
evidence.explanation: Supports the engineered sucrose-export capacity; exact partner growth and condition boundaries are recorded separately.

evidence.snippet: E. coli strains cannot utilize sucrose effectively and dominantly depend on other metabolites from S. elongatus
evidence.explanation: Source inference for early low-sucrose growth; does not identify a measured alternative carbon species.

changed_graph.name: E. coli growth on cyanobacterial photosynthate
changed_graph.description: E. coli W delta-cscR grew on cyanobacterial photosynthate and maintained viability in continuous coculture for more than two weeks. Early batch growth was not primarily attributable to sucrose export; improved sucrose utilization contributed to later PHB production in separately functionalized strains. No product-removal feedback mechanism establishing syntrophy is shown by carbon feeding alone.

downstream.target: E. coli Stimulation of Cyanobacterial Growth
downstream.description: HYPOTHESIZED/PARTIAL: photosynthate-supported heterotroph activity could contribute to the observed cyanobacterial growth benefit through metabolite return or byproduct absorption. The study does not isolate sucrose uptake as its cause or identify a necessary exchanged compound; positive and negative effects depend on culture context.

evidence.snippet: we determined that co-cultures maintain stable ratios for more than two weeks
evidence.explanation: Primary Results identifies these continuous cultures as W delta-cscR paired with cscB+ S. elongatus, not every E. coli background.

biological_processes.notes: Capacity and condition-dependent utilization; not an exclusive explanation of all coculture growth.

changed_graph.name: E. coli Stimulation of Cyanobacterial Growth
changed_graph.description: The tested heterotrophic partner increased cyanobacterial abundance relative to axenic controls in low-density cocultures. Together with photosynthate-supported heterotroph growth, this supports conditional reciprocal benefit. It is not universal stability: dense illuminated cyanobacteria could inhibit heterotroph viability. The source proposes metabolite return or byproduct absorption as possible explanations for stimulation, without resolving the mediator; respiratory CO2 alone was considered questionable.

evidence.snippet: inoculation of each heterotrophic species enhanced cyanobacterial growth
evidence.explanation: Supports the measured heterotroph-associated cyanobacterial growth increase, not its exact mediator or unconditional mutualism.

evidence.snippet: all three evolutionarily unrelated heterotrophs can significantly increase cyanobacterial growth under a range of growth conditions
